content: The MS Bike Tour, also known as the MS 150, is a series of charity cycling events organized by the National Multiple Sclerosis Society in the United States, Canada, and Australia. These events aim to raise funds for research into multiple sclerosis (MS) and to support those affected by the disease. In the United States, the rides are branded as MS 150 and typically span two days, covering approximately 150 miles. However, shorter one-day rides are also available. The routes are designed to start and end in major cities to maximize accessibility and participation. The number of participants varies by event, with some rides, such as the Houston-to-Austin route, attracting up to 13,000 riders. In Australia, the event is known as Sydney to the Gong, referring to the 90-kilometer ride from Sydney to Wollongong. Multiple sclerosis (MS) is a chronic autoimmune disease that targets the central nervous system (CNS). It damages the myelin sheath, which insulates and protects nerve fibers, leading to the formation of lesions known as sclerosis. The symptoms of MS are highly variable and unpredictable, ranging from vision loss and paralysis to numbness and difficulty walking. These symptoms can fluctuate, making diagnosis challenging. The National Multiple Sclerosis Society, established in 1946, is dedicated to combating MS through research, education, advocacy, and support services. The MS Bike Tours, which began over two decades ago, are among the organization's most significant fundraising initiatives. These events now take place in 48 U.S. states and several locations in Canada, with distances ranging from 30 to 180 miles. Participants can contribute by cycling, volunteering, or pledging donations. The events foster community involvement, drawing support from local businesses, officials, residents, and individuals living with MS. Approximately 75% of the funds raised go directly toward research. In North America, the MS Bike Tours are supported by 48 state chapters, with over 100,000 participants raising $67 million in 2006 alone. In Canada, 10,000 participants raised $7.1 million in the same year. The tours, which run from April to November, are tailored to the needs and capabilities of each local chapter, allowing for flexibility in route length, dates, and locations. The largest event is the Lone Star Chapter's BP MS 150, a two-day ride from Houston to Austin, which has raised over $47 million to date. Other notable events in Texas include the Sam’s Club MS 150 from Frisco to Fort Worth in May and the Valero MS 150 from San Antonio to Corpus Christi in October. These events are strategically designed to attract media attention and public support. In Australia, the annual Sydney to the Gong ride offers two distance options: a 90-kilometer route from St. Peters in Sydney to Stuart Park in Wollongong, and a shorter 56-kilometer route from Heathcote High School to Stuart Park. The event typically takes place in early November. In 2006, 100,000 riders participated in the MS Bike Tours, collectively raising $67 million. Riders face the physical and emotional challenge of cycling to support the fight against MS. Participants range in age from 6 to 82 years old and use a variety of bicycles, including traditional road bikes, tandem bikes, recumbent bikes, hand-operated cycles, and even unicycles. Safety is a top priority, with all events adhering to the National MS Society's safety guidelines and local laws. Roads and trails are secured, and helmets are mandatory. Police, volunteers, and HAM radio operators are stationed along the routes to provide assistance, while rest stops offer medical services, refreshments, technical support, and bathrooms. Riders must pledge a minimum fundraising amount to participate, with requirements varying by chapter. To incentivize fundraising, some chapters recognize top fundraisers with membership in exclusive clubs. The Champions Against MS program pairs riders with individuals living with MS, fostering a personal connection and raising awareness through the symbolic red bandana signed by the MS buddy. Volunteers play a crucial role in the success of the MS Bike Tours, often matching or exceeding the number of riders. They handle event setup, cleanup, and logistics, as well as provide support and encouragement to participants. Volunteers may take on unique roles such as team cooks, masseuses, or bike rack attendants. HAM radio operators facilitate communication along the route. Volunteers are known for their enthusiasm, often dressing in colorful costumes and using noisemakers to motivate riders. The MS Bike Tours have garnered support from numerous celebrities over the years. Country singer Clay Walker, diagnosed with MS in 1996, participates in the BP MS 150 and inspires others with his resilience. Texas Governor Rick Perry and Houston Mayor Bill White joined the BP MS 150 in 2004, with Perry riding the final 10 miles and White completing the entire route. Talk show host Montel Williams, who revealed his MS diagnosis in 1999, founded his own MS bike tour in New York. Other notable supporters include singer Alan Osmond, comedian Jonathan Katz, and actress Lena Horne. Local celebrities, such as government officials and media personalities, also contribute to the events. Corporate sponsors provide significant financial and logistical support for the MS Bike Tours. Sponsorship levels range from title sponsors, who make the largest contributions, to platinum, gold, silver, and bronze sponsors. Local businesses, radio stations, transportation companies, and hotels also contribute by offering services or financial support. Sponsors often set up tents at finish lines, providing food, beverages, and amenities such as massages for riders. Riders affiliated with sponsor companies may wear branded jerseys, further promoting the sponsors' involvement in the fight against MS.
